children: To the Editor: Sales of nonalcoholic beer aren't low because it doesn't taste like beer; they're low because it doesn't have any alcohol in it ("This Stock's for You: Buy Bud's 'Diet Coke' Moment," Cover Story, Oct. 14). I've been to Leuven, Belgium, many times. There are lots of bars, and the locals get it. Evidently, execs don't. If the thesis is that nonalcoholic beer is going to save Anheuser-Busch InBev, I'll fade it all day, every day. Here's another idea: Don't anger your customers with your marketing campaigns.

To the Editor: Taxation of the ultrarich is a difficult subject to agree upon, and probably always will be ("Taxes on the Wealthy Are on the Ballot in Many States. Could It Become a Federal Trend?" Oct. 15). But states need to be careful in how they go about it. If we tax the wealthy based on their assets, does that mean the government goes into their homes and assesses the value of their paintings, cars, and jewelry, or makes them open their safe-deposit boxes to determine the value of the items within? A tax where those with very large incomes pay their fair amount is easier to monitor than to try taxing wealth. We just need to agree upon the definition of a very large income and decide on a fair amount.
Thomas J. Kloepfer Buffalo Grove, Ill.

To the Editor: John D. Rockefeller understood something that many investors have forgotten: Dividends are among the clearest expressions of shareholder ownership ("The S&P 500's Dividend Yield Is at an All-Time Low. What to Do If You're an Income Investor," Oct. 15). From a shareholder's perspective, a corporation is ultimately a machine for converting invested capital into sustainable cash distributions. While buybacks have their place, dividends represent a recurring financial commitment to shareholders. More importantly, dividend increases are among the loudest and clearest signals that management can send about its confidence in future earnings and cash flows. The S&P 500 index's historically low yield doesn't make dividends obsolete. It makes dividend discipline more important than ever.

To the Editor:The propensity for a product or service to decrease in price is inversely proportional to the percentage of labor in said product or service ("Bond Investors See Inflation Cooling. Consumers See Anything But," The Economy, Oct. 16). In other words, because wages have a sticky upward bias, the higher the percentage of labor in a product or service, the less the price will come down when other comprising costs are reduced.
